:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, to find $A^2,$ we multiply $A$ by itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $A^4 = A^2 \cdot A^2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & ={A}^{2}\cdot {A}^{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}81 & 0 \\ 100 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Power of a Matrix

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & =-{X}^{2}+3X+2 \\  & =-{X}^{2}+3X+2I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(D)=-D^2+3D+2I.$

Let's calculate $D^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(D)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & =-{D}^{2}+3D+2I \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 10 \\ 0 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 15 \\ 0 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1+3+2 & 10+15+0 \\ 0 & -9-9+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 25 \\ 0 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
